citations.location: Fifth Affirmative Defense: Statute of Limitations (line 169)
citations.cited_for: Under Michigan law, fraud claims are subject to a six-year statute of limitations.
citations.context: Under Michigan law, fraud claims are subject to a six-year statute of limitations pursuant to MCL § 600.5813. However, the discovery rule codified at MCL § 600.5855 requires that such claims be brought within two years of the date the plaintiff discovered

first_check.explanation: MCL 600.5813 is Michigan's residual six-year limitations period for 'all other personal actions'. The Michigan Supreme Court (Boyle v General Motors, 468 Mich 226 (2003)) treats it as the six-year period that governs fraud actions. The proposition is accurate. Only the Answer's next clause, about § 600.5855, is wrong (see ref 1).
first_check.evidence_excerpt: "All other personal actions shall be commenced within the period of 6 years after the claims accrue and not afterwards unless a different period is stated in the statutes." ... Boyle: "MCL 600.5813 and 600.5855, the six-year statute of limitations applicable to fraud actions and the fraudulent-concealment statute"

citations.location: Fifth Affirmative Defense: Statute of Limitations (line 169)
citations.cited_for: Described as the 'discovery rule codified' requiring fraudulent concealment claims be brought within two years of the date the plaintiff discovered, or should have discovered, the claim.
citations.context: the discovery rule codified at MCL § 600.5855 requires that such claims be brought within two years of the date the plaintiff discovered, or through the exercise of reasonable diligence should have discovered, the existence of the claim.

first_check.explanation: MCL 600.5855 is a fraudulent-concealment savings provision, not a general codified discovery rule. It applies only when the liable party fraudulently concealed the claim or the identity of the liable person. In that case it extends the time to sue to 2 years after discovery, 'although the action would otherwise be barred.' The Answer gets this backwards: it says § 600.5855 'requires' fraud claims to be brought within two years of discovery, presented as a limit that cuts the six-year period short. Boyle confirms the statute only allows concealed claims to be brought late.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: If a person who is or may be liable for any claim fraudulently conceals the existence of the claim ... the action may be commenced at any time within 2 years after the person who is entitled to bring the action discovers, or should have discovered, the existence of the claim ... although the action would otherwise be barred by the period of limitations.

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. MCL 600.5855 is headed 'Fraudulent concealment of claim or identity of person liable; discovery.' Its text says that if a liable person 'fraudulently conceals the existence of the claim ... the action may be commenced at any time within 2 years after the person who is entitled to bring the action discovers, or should have discovered, the existence of the claim ... although the action would otherwise be barred by the period of limitations.' So it is a savings and extension provision that applies only where the claim was fraudulently concealed. It is not a general codified discovery rule that shortens the six-year fraud limitations period. The Answer presents it as a rule requiring fraud claims to be brought within two years of discovery, which reverses its function.

citations.location: Section II. Firm Policy on Boilerplate Objections, final paragraph (line 37)
citations.cited_for: Requires responses to requests for production be served within 35 days after service of the requests unless court orders or parties stipulate otherwise.
citations.context: MCR 2.310(B) requires that responses to requests for production be served within 35 days after service of the requests, unless the court orders otherwise or the parties stipulate in writing to a different schedule.

first_check.explanation: There are two errors. First, MCR 2.310(B) is the 'Scope' subrule and sets no deadline; the response deadline is in MCR 2.310(C)(2). Second, the current rule sets 28 days after service of the request, not 35 (a defendant may instead respond within 42 days after being served with the summons and complaint). The court may allow a longer or shorter time. The rule as stated in the playbook gives the wrong deadline.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: The party on whom the request is served must serve a written response within 28 days after service of the request, except that a defendant may serve a response within 42 days after being served with the summons and complaint. The court may allow a longer or shorter time.

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. In the current official text of MCR 2.310, subrule (B) is headed 'Scope' and covers only what a party or nonparty may be asked to produce; it sets no deadline. The timing rule is in (C)(2): 'The party on whom the request is served must serve a written response within 28 days after service of the request, except that a defendant may serve a response within 42 days after being served with the summons and complaint. The court may allow a longer or shorter time.' The rule contains no 35-day period and no written-stipulation language. So the playbook's statement is wrong on both the subrule and the deadline. The correct citation is MCR 2.310(C)(2), with 28 days.

citations.cited_for: Every response to a request for production must state whether documents are being withheld on the basis of an objection.

first_check.explanation: MCR 2.310(C)(2) requires each response to say that inspection will be permitted or that the request is objected to, give the reasons for any objection, and specify the part objected to. Nowhere does it require a response to state whether documents are being withheld because of an objection. That requirement comes from Fed. R. Civ. P. 34(b)(2)(C), not the Michigan rule. A search of the whole of MCR Chapter 2 for 'withh' found no such requirement in MCR 2.302 or 2.310.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: With respect to each item or category, the response must state that inspection and related activities will be permitted as requested or that the request is objected to, in which event the reasons for objection must be stated. If objection is made to part of an item or category, the part must be specified.

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. I read the full text of MCR 2.310. The closest language is in (C)(2): 'With respect to each item or category, the response must state that inspection and related activities will be permitted as requested or that the request is objected to, in which event the reasons for objection must be stated. If objection is made to part of an item or category, the part must be specified.' Nothing in it requires a response to state whether documents are being withheld on the basis of an objection; that requirement is the federal Rule 34(b)(2)(C) language. I searched the whole of Chapter 2 of the Michigan Court Rules for 'withh'. The only hit was an unrelated garnishment provision. On a fair reading, the Michigan rule does not support the stated 'critical compliance point.'

citations.cited_for: ESI production format (native or TIFF with extracted text and metadata)
citations.context: including custodian information, file path, date created, date modified, date sent, date received, author, recipients, and subject line, in accordance with MCR 2.310(B).

first_check.explanation: MCR 2.310(B) (scope) does not address ESI format. The format provisions are in (C)(1) and (C)(2). (C)(1) says the request must specify the form or forms for producing ESI, subject to objection. (C)(2) sets a default form when the request specifies none. The rule does not itself require native or TIFF production with metadata. Read fairly, though, a requester's specified format is 'in accordance with' the rule, because the rule authorizes the requester to name one. The subrule is wrong and the support is loose.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: The request must specify a reasonable time, place, and manner of making the inspection and performing the related acts, as well as the form or forms in which electronically stored information is to be produced, subject to objection.

citations.cited_for: Requests are continuing; duty to supplement responses
citations.context: These Requests are continuing in nature pursuant to MCR 2.302(E). If, after Your initial response, You obtain, discover, or become aware of additional responsive Documents or ESI, You are obligated to supplement Your response promptly

first_check.explanation: MCR 2.302(E), 'Supplementing Disclosures and Responses', requires a party that has answered a request for production to supplement or correct its response in a timely manner when it learns the response is materially incomplete or incorrect. That supports the instruction that the requests are continuing and responses must be supplemented. Calling the requests 'continuing in nature' is a common shorthand, and the rule supports it.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: (1) Duty to Supplement. (a) In General. A party that has made a disclosure under MCR 2.302(A)—or that has responded to an interrogatory, request for production, or request for admission—must supplement or correct its disclosure or response: (i) in a timely manner if the party learns that in some material respect the disclosure or response is incomplete or incorrect

citations.cited_for: Documents may be produced as kept in usual course of business or organized by request
citations.context: they shall be organized and labeled to correspond with each individual Request to which they are responsive, as permitted by MCR 2.310(B)(1).

first_check.explanation: The substance is right: a producing party may produce documents as kept in the usual course of business, or organize and label them to match the request's categories. That rule is MCR 2.310(C)(5), not (B)(1). (B)(1) sets the scope of requests to parties. The subrule is wrong.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: (5) A party who produces documents for inspection shall produce them as they are kept in the usual course of business or shall organize and label them to correspond with the categories in the request.

citations.context: to be served upon counsel for Defendant via electronic service at the email address listed below, in accordance with MCR 2.107(C)(4)

first_check.explanation: MCR 2.107(C)(4), 'Alternative Electronic Service', allows parties to agree to service among themselves by e-mail by filing a stipulation. It supports e-mail service on counsel, though it assumes such a stipulation exists; the document does not say whether one was filed.

Alternative electronic service may be by any of the following methods: (i) e-mail

citations.authority: Michigan Court Rules (clawback of inadvertently produced privileged document)
citations.cited_for: Clawback demand for inadvertently produced privileged email REDFIELD-000847 may be warranted under the Michigan Court Rules
citations.context: Counsel should promptly evaluate whether a clawback demand is warranted under the applicable Michigan Court Rules or any existing clawback agreement or protective order governing this litigation.

first_check.explanation: This is a generic reference. MCR 2.302(B)(7) ('Information Inadvertently Produced') lets the producing party notify the receiving party of a privilege claim over inadvertently produced material, which triggers a duty to return, sequester or destroy it. That supports evaluating a clawback demand under the Michigan Court Rules.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: If information that is subject to a claim of privilege or of protection as trial-preparation material is produced in discovery, the party making the claim may notify any party that received the information of the claim and the basis for it. After being notified, a party must promptly return, sequester, or destroy the specified information

citations.cited_for: Order analogous to FRE 502(d) could govern inadvertent disclosures; unknown whether one has been entered
citations.context: Pinnacle is not aware of whether a stipulated clawback agreement, protective order, or any order analogous to Federal Rule of Evidence 502(d) has been entered in this matter.

first_check.explanation: FRE 502(d) lets a federal court order that disclosure in connection with the pending litigation does not waive privilege. Describing a non-waiver/clawback order as 'analogous to FRE 502(d)' is accurate.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: A federal court may order that the privilege or protection is not waived by disclosure connected with the litigation pending before the court

citations.cited_for: Memo should discuss clawback mechanism for inadvertent production (Michigan's clawback framework, MCR provisions)
citations.context: (e.g., referencing Michigan's clawback framework, MCR provisions, or the need to promptly notify opposing counsel and demand return/destruction)

first_check.explanation: Generic rubric reference to 'Michigan's clawback framework, MCR provisions'. MCR 2.302(B)(7) ('Information Inadvertently Produced') is that framework. It lets the privilege holder notify the receiving party, which must then promptly return, sequester or destroy the information. That matches the rubric's description (prompt notice; demand for return or destruction).
first_check.evidence_excerpt: MCR 2.302(B)(7): "If information that is subject to a claim of privilege or of protection as trial-preparation material is produced in discovery, the party making the claim may notify any party that received the information of the claim and the basis for it. After being notified, a party must promptly return, sequester, or destroy the specified information..."

citations.cited_for: Proportionality objection to Request No. 6 (all ESI)
citations.context: raises a proportionality objection, referencing the burden of the request relative to the needs of the case, or citing MCR 2.302(B)(1) or proportionality principles.

first_check.explanation: MCR 2.302(B)(1) limits discovery to matter 'proportional to the needs of the case' and lists burden versus benefit among the factors. It supports a proportionality objection to a request for all ESI.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: Parties may obtain discovery regarding any non-privileged matter that is relevant to any party's claims or defenses and proportional to the needs of the case, taking into account all pertinent factors, including whether the burden or expense of the proposed discovery outweighs its likely benefit

citations.cited_for: Proportionality factors / balancing test for ESI discovery burdens
citations.context: references Michigan Court Rule 2.302(B)(1) proportionality factors or the balancing test for ESI discovery burdens (e.g., importance of issues, amount in controversy, parties' resources, importance of discovery to resolving issues, burden vs. likely benefit, or reasonable accessibility). FAIL if neither document references MCR 2.302(B)(1)

first_check.correct_citation: MCR 2.302(B)(1); see also MCR 2.302(B)(6) (ESI not reasonably accessible)
first_check.explanation: MCR 2.302(B)(1) does set out proportionality factors. The rule lists burden or expense versus likely benefit, complexity of the case, importance of the issues, amount in controversy, and the parties' resources and access to information. The rubric's example list is loose in two ways. It includes 'importance of discovery to resolving issues', a factor from FRCP 26(b)(1) that the Michigan rule omits. It also includes 'reasonable accessibility', which comes from MCR 2.302(B)(6), not (B)(1). The core point, proportionality factors under (B)(1), is accurate.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: taking into account all pertinent factors, including whether the burden or expense of the proposed discovery outweighs its likely benefit, the complexity of the case, the importance of the issues at stake in the action, the amount in controversy, and the parties' resources and access to relevant information.

citations.cited_for: Objections should cite applicable Michigan Court Rules as legal basis
citations.context: PASS if at least some objections cite or reference applicable Michigan Court Rules (e.g., MCR 2.310, MCR 2.302, or other MCR provisions) as the legal basis for the objection.

first_check.explanation: Both rules are proper legal bases for objections to production requests. MCR 2.310(C) governs responses to production requests and requires a stated reason for each objection. MCR 2.302 sets the scope of discovery, including relevance, proportionality and privilege under (B)(1), and the limits on discovery of ESI.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: With respect to each item or category, the response must state that inspection and related activities will be permitted as requested or that the request is objected to, in which event the reasons for objection must be stated.
